title: Hugh Hoskins' club: pimps, pickpockets and Tack Annie
summary: After Dago Frank's was closed she went to the tiny Hoskins club, where pianist Zella Hunter played and pimps, sporting girls and pickpockets like Tack Annie hung out; Lumsie tried to pawn a picture of Jesus.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Well, listen, here's what I want to say. You don't want to come up to -- did I tell you all about Hugh Hoskins down at 32nd Street and all that?
Oh, boy. Well, you know, after I got the job at Dago Frank's, you know --
Well, when Dago Frank's -- they closed the place because it was kind of a red light district, you know, and you know what that is.
Well, anyhow, when they closed the
place, why I went up to a place called Hugh Hoskin's. That was a little, tiny club not any bigger than, well, about the size of this room.
And had a pianist by the name of Zella Hunter. She could really play piano. No relation. But she was marvelous, and that's where most all the -- can I say pimps?
That's where all the pimps and the sporting girls and the pickpocket women and all hung out. So they -- there was one there called Tack Annie. I know you've heard of her.

She could steal a nickel off a dead man's eye. She was somebody. Tack Annie, Alabama Mary, Lumsie. Lumsie was a fellow. He was one of the pimps. And Lumsie used to pawn everything, you know, everything he'd get his hands on he'd go and pawn it, you know. So Lumsie got down to the last thing and he had a photograph of the Lord. So Lumsie took that to the pawnshop, and they told Lumsie, said, 'Listen Lumsie, you've brought everything in here, but we are not going to let you pawn Jesus Christ.'
